text: "Unworthily" describes the manner, not the person. The Lord's Supper was never meant to keep you away; it was meant for you.
explanation:
Many believers were taught not to come to the Lord's table if there's sin in their life, and some stayed away for months out of fear. But Paul uses an adverb: whoever eats "in an unworthy manner." An adverb modifies the action, not the actor. Paul isn't asking whether you are worthy; he is asking how you are taking it.

The Corinthians were turning the meal into a feast where some got drunk and others went hungry. They were going through the motions without recognising what the elements meant. Jesus' body was broken for sinners, the sick and the needy. If you were already whole, you wouldn't need a Healer.

text: The cup is for your forgiveness. The broken bread is for your healing.
explanation:
Paul gives one reason many believers were weak, sick and dying early: "not discerning the Lord's body." He doesn't mention the blood. The Corinthians understood that the blood forgives, but missed what the broken body was for.

Read it in reverse and it becomes a promise: discern the Lord's body, and for this reason many are strong, healthy and live long. When you hold the bread, don't just remember that He died; receive what His body was broken to give. "Lord, Your body was broken so that mine can be whole."

text: Passover matzah is striped, pierced and burnt: a picture of the One by whose stripes we are healed.
explanation:
The unleavened bread used at Passover has stripes across it, holes pierced through it, and burn marks from the fire. Leaven speaks of sin, so the bread must be unleavened, just as Jesus was without sin.

When Jesus held up that bread and said "This is My body, broken for you," every mark meant something. His back bore the stripes, His hands and feet were pierced, and the fire of judgment meant for us fell on Him instead. He was burned so that you never will be; He took the stripes so that you could be healed.

text: God never separated forgiveness from healing. "Who forgives all your iniquities, who heals all your diseases."
explanation:
Isaiah 53 shows both happening at the cross: He was wounded for our transgressions, and by His stripes we are healed. Matthew confirms it, quoting Isaiah: "He Himself took our infirmities and bore our sicknesses." Over and over in the Gospels, Jesus forgives and heals in the same stroke.

That's why there are two elements at the Lord's table. People have pulled forgiveness and healing apart, so many are forgiven but stay sick. God put them together. The same Saviour who washed away all your sins also bore all your diseases.

text: To confess (homologeo) means to say the same thing God says: it was sin, and it is forgiven by Jesus' blood.
explanation:
Some teaching turns confession into an endless search through your past: sins you committed, sins you omitted, even sins passed down from your ancestors. However much you confess, a nagging doubt remains that you missed something.

The Greek "homologeo" combines "homo" (same) and "logeo" (to speak). It means agreeing with God, and God says two things about your sins: they were sin, and Jesus' blood has forgiven them all, past, present and future. When you take the cup, thank Him for that. That's where peace comes from.

text: Healing didn't depend on how good their eyes were. It only required that they look.
explanation:
When the Israelites were dying from snake bites, God told Moses to set a bronze serpent on a pole. Anyone bitten who looked at it lived. God didn't ask them to examine their eyes first. Tired eyes, weak eyes, one eye half-open: whoever looked was healed.

Jesus said He would be lifted up the same way. Bronze speaks of judgment; your sickness was judged on that cross. The only thing you can't do is look at the cross and your wound at the same time, so take your eyes off yourself and look to Him.

text: It's hard to tempt someone who knows they're loved.
explanation:
At the Jordan the Father said, "This is My beloved Son." Straight afterwards, in the wilderness, the devil said, "If You are the Son of God…" and dropped the word "beloved." He knows his first move has to be making you feel unloved, dirty or rejected.

People don't usually fall into sin out of nowhere. First they believe nobody cares, then the temptation lands. The enemy works by deception because he has no real power over you. When you know you are God's beloved, that first step never gets a foothold.

text: Don't chase health. Don't chase wealth. Chase Jesus, and He brings both.
explanation:
When Israel left Egypt, God brought them out with silver and gold, "and there was none feeble among His tribes." That's health and wealth together, under a covenant founded on the blood of animals. How much more under a better covenant, founded on the blood of God's own Son?

Yet health and wealth were never the goal. Wherever Jesus went, the sick were healed, nets broke with fish, and thousands were fed from a boy's lunch. Those blessings followed Him. Go after Jesus Himself, and what you need comes with Him.
